name: Abdiel
title: Man in the genealogy of the tribe of Gad
summary: Abdiel appears in the genealogy of Gad's tribe in Chronicles, where he is identified as the son of Guni and father of Ahi – the latter mentioned as head of his clan. The family belonged to the Transjordanian region of Gilead in Bashan, an area known for its fertile pastures and strategic location. The name Abdiel carries the meaning 'servant of God' and reflects a widespread Israelite tradition of theophoric personal names expressing devotion to the God of Israel. The recording of this genealogy is linked to the reigns of Jotham of Judah and Jeroboam II of Israel, an overlapping period around the mid-700s BC characterized by relative prosperity. Abdiel's presence in the text – though brief – underscores the importance that Israelite authors placed on preserving every link in the tribes' collective identity and history.

keyEvents.title: Mentioned in the genealogy of Gad
keyEvents.description: Abdiel is listed as the son of Guni in the genealogy of the tribe of Gad. His son Ahi held the position of head of his clan, and the family lived in Gilead, in Bashan and its surrounding towns.

keyEvents.title: Settlements of the tribe of Gad in Gilead
keyEvents.description: Abdiel's clan and the other descendants of Gad settled in Gilead in Bashan and in the pastures of Sharon as far as they extended—an area known for its fertility and importance to the tribe.

keyEvents.title: Genealogical record during Jotham and Jeroboam
keyEvents.description: The genealogy that includes Abdiel was recorded during the reigns of Jotham, king of Judah, and Jeroboam II, king of Israel, placing the record in a period of relative prosperity around the middle of the 8th century BC.

versions.title: Descendant of Gad
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'Descendant of Gad' is slightly imprecise. Abdiel is not a direct descendant of Gad in the sense that he is Gad's son, but rather a person listed in the genealogy of the tribe of Gad. A more accurate title would be 'Man of the Tribe of Gad' or 'Member of the Tribe of Gad'.; [major] The role 'leader' is not supported by the biblical text. 1 Chron 5:15 states that Ahi, son of Abdiel, son of Guni, was 'head of his clan'. Thus it is Ahi who is called head/leader, not Abdiel. Abdiel has no specified role beyond being mentioned in the genealogy. A more appropriate role would be 'ancestor' or 'clan member'.; [minor] The summary is mostly good, but it should clarify that according to 1 Chron 5:15 it was Ahi (Abdiel's son) who was head of his family, not Abdiel himself. The wording should also make clear Abdiel's place in the genealogical chain.; [minor] The last two events (verses 16-18) concern the tribe of Gad generally and are not directly linked to Abdiel as an individual. It is acceptable to include them for context, but the descriptions should clarify that this is tribal history rather than personal biography.; [minor] Footnotes are missing. A linguistic note on the meaning of the name Abdiel ('servant of God'), as well as a historical note about the genealogical registration during the time of Jotham and Jeroboam II, would have been useful.

versions.summary:
Abdiel is mentioned in the Chronicles' overview of the tribe of Gad as the son of Guni and father of Ahi.  
Ahi held the role of head of his clan, and the family was settled in the fertile Gilead region of Bashan east of the Jordan.  
The name Abdiel – meaning 'servant of God' – carries within it a testimony of faith and devotion to the God of Israel.  
The recording of this lineage likely took place around 750 BC, during the overlapping reigns of Jotham and Jeroboam II, a time marked by relative stability.  
Although Abdiel appears only briefly in the text, his place in the genealogy serves as an important link in preserving the history of the tribe of Gad and Israel's collective memory.

footnotes.text: The name Abdiel (עַבְדִּיאֵל) is composed of the Hebrew words 'eved' (עֶבֶד, servant) and 'El' (אֵל, God), meaning 'servant of God.' Such theophoric names—names containing a divine element—were common in ancient Israel and reflect a conscious tradition of piety. Similar name forms are also found in other Semitic cultures.

The genealogy in 1 Chron 5:17 dates the recording to the reigns of Jotham, king of Judah (ca. 750–735 B.C.), and Jeroboam II, king of Israel (ca. 793–753 B.C.). The overlapping period around 750 B.C. was marked by relative political stability and economic prosperity in both kingdoms, which may have enabled administrative projects such as tribal registration.

Gilead and Bashan were fertile regions east of the Jordan River, known for grazing lands, forests, and rich agricultural production. Archaeological surveys in the region have uncovered widespread settlement activity from the Iron Age (ca. 1200–586 B.C.), which aligns with biblical descriptions of Israelite tribes living in the area.

According to 1 Chron 5:15, it was Ahi, Abdiel's son, who was 'head' (Hebrew: ראש, rosh) of his clan. The term rosh is consistently used in the Hebrew Bible for clan leaders, tribal heads, and other authorities, indicating a formal and recognized leadership position within Israel's tribal structure.

The tribe of Gad was among the Transjordanian tribes that received their territories during Joshua's conquest. This location made them vulnerable to attacks from neighboring peoples, which, according to 1 Chron 5:18–22, led them to develop a strong military tradition. The context surrounding Abdiel's family shows that tribal affiliation was not only genealogical but also had practical significance for defense and land management.

In rabbinic tradition, the genealogies in Chronicles are regarded as important testimonies of God's faithfulness to His people. Even brief entries like Abdiel's confirm that each lineage was considered valuable and worth preserving, as an expression of the covenant relationship between God and Israel.
